sections: The metric (SI) system is based on powers of ten, which makes conversions inside it easy: 1 km = 1,000 m = 100,000 cm. The imperial and US customary systems use historic units (12 inches to a foot, 3 feet to a yard, 16 ounces to a pound). Only the United States, Liberia and Myanmar mainly use non-metric units in daily life, while the UK uses a mix – miles on road signs, stones for body weight, litres for fuel.

Some units with the same name differ: a US gallon is 3.785 L but an imperial gallon is 4.546 L; a US fluid ounce is 29.57 mL, an imperial one 28.41 mL; a US (short) ton is 907 kg, a UK (long) ton 1,016 kg and a metric tonne 1,000 kg. Check which one a recipe or specification means.

Every factor is the exact legal definition published by NIST and the international SI system – for example 1 inch = 2.54 cm exactly, 1 pound = 0.45359237 kg exactly and 1 mile = 1,609.344 m – so results are as precise as the numbers you type. Temperatures use offset formulas rather than a single factor. The formula used is shown under every result so you can check it or reuse it in a spreadsheet.

sections: Height is often written as feet and inches, e.g. 5 ft 8 in. Convert the feet to inches (5 × 12 = 60), add the inches (68 in), then multiply by 2.54: 172.7 cm. Going the other way, 180 cm ÷ 2.54 = 70.87 in = 5 ft 10.9 in. For quick lookups use [cm to inches](/cm-to-inches/), [inches to cm](/inches-to-cm/) or [feet to metres](/feet-to-meters/).

sections: Quick mental check: double the Celsius and add 30 for an approximate Fahrenheit (20 °C ≈ 70 °F; exact 68 °F).

Recipes from the US use Fahrenheit, from the UK, India and Europe Celsius (sometimes gas marks). 350 °F ≈ 175–180 °C, 400 °F ≈ 200 °C, 425 °F ≈ 220 °C. Fan (convection) ovens usually need 10–20 °C less than conventional ovens.

Weather forecasts in the US use °F: 90 °F is a hot 32 °C, 32 °F is freezing. A body temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or more is usually considered a fever in adults; check medical advice for children. sections: Why does my 1 TB drive show 931 GB?

Drive makers use decimal units: 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Windows counts in binary units but labels them GB: 10¹² ÷ 1,073,741,824 = 931.3 'GB' (really GiB). Nothing is missing. macOS has used decimal units since 2009, so it shows 1 TB.

Internet speeds are quoted in bits per second; file sizes in bytes. 1 byte = 8 bits, so a 100 Mbit/s connection downloads at most 12.5 MB per second, and a 1 GB file takes at least 80 seconds. Upload limits and phone data plans use bytes.

sections: Time zone converter and meeting planner

Find out what time it is – or will be – anywhere in the world. Enter a date and time, choose its zone and the zones you want, and get exact results that account for daylight saving on that date. sections: Abbreviations are ambiguous – IST also means Irish and Israel Standard Time – so the converter uses city-based IANA zones such as Asia/Kolkata.

Zones are named after a representative city (America/New_York, Europe/London) because rules change over time and between regions in the same country. Picking the city avoids mistakes such as treating Arizona (no daylight saving) like the rest of US Mountain Time.
How time zones and daylight saving are handled

The converter uses the IANA time-zone database built into your browser – the same data used by phones, operating systems and calendar apps – so daylight-saving changes, historical rule changes and half-hour or 45-minute offsets (India, Nepal, parts of Australia) are always applied for the exact date you choose. It warns you when clocks change in the next 12 months for the zones you picked.

Below the result, an hour-by-hour table shows the same moment in every selected zone with 9:00–17:00 working hours highlighted, and the overlap of working hours is calculated for you. Use *Copy link* to share the exact time with colleagues – the link opens the converter with your zones and time already filled in.

list: Always write the zone with the time: 10:00 IST / 21:30 PDT.
Prefer UTC in technical work, logs and server schedules.
Remember that the US and Europe change clocks on different dates in March and October/November, so offsets shift for a few weeks.
India, China, Japan and most of Asia and Africa do not use daylight saving.

sections: The most frequent scheduling error is assuming a fixed difference all year. Between the second Sunday of March and the last Sunday of March, for example, the US has already moved its clocks forward while Europe has not, so New York is four hours behind London instead of five. Another trap is the date line: when it is Monday morning in India or Australia it can still be Sunday afternoon or evening in the Americas. Finally, avoid writing ambiguous times such as 12:00 am – use 00:00 or midnight, or a 24-hour clock, and always add the zone. The converter shows dates next to each time to make day changes obvious.

Distributed teams often pick a few shared hours for meetings and keep the rest for focused work. Use the working-hours table to find that window, then put it in team calendars. Freelancers serving clients abroad can paste a shared link into proposals so clients see call slots in their own time.

India's late evening overlaps with California's morning. A 9:00 am PDT stand-up is 9:30 pm IST; 8:00 am PST is 9:30 pm IST in winter. Morning slots in India (8–10 am IST) reach the US West Coast the previous evening (7:30–9:30 pm PDT).
Because the gap is more than 12 hours, an Indian morning is the previous calendar day in California. Always state the date with the time when scheduling.

seo.title: TTF to WOFF2 Converter – Web Fonts Free, No Upload
seo.desc: Convert TTF or OTF fonts to WOFF2 (or WOFF) for faster websites – about 30–50 % smaller, same glyphs. Batch, free, in your browser, no upload.
sections: WOFF2 is the web-font format every modern browser supports. It packs the same glyphs as your TTF or OTF file with Brotli compression, typically making fonts 30–50 % smaller so pages load faster and text appears sooner. Convert one single font or a whole family here, with Google's reference woff2 encoder running in your browser.

steps: Drop one or more TTF or OTF files.
Keep WOFF2 (or choose WOFF for very old browsers, or TTF/OTF to convert back).
Press Convert and download.

sections: Upload the .woff2 file and reference it in CSS with an @font-face rule: set font-family, point src to url('/fonts/name.woff2') with format('woff2'), and add font-display: swap so text shows immediately in a fallback font. Preload the most important font with a link rel=preload tag. Every browser released since about 2016 supports WOFF2, so a WOFF fallback is rarely needed today.

Converting does not change a font's licence. Many commercial desktop licences do not permit web embedding; check the EULA or buy a web licence. Open-source fonts under the SIL Open Font License (most Google Fonts) may be converted and self-hosted freely.

Subsetting – keeping only the characters you use, such as Latin only – can cut a font by a further 50–90 %. Use a desktop tool such as pyftsubset or glyphhanger for that, then convert here. Variable fonts in one WOFF2 can replace several static weights.

Fonts are often among the largest files on a page. Smaller fonts improve Largest Contentful Paint and reduce layout shift when combined with font-display and size-adjusted fallbacks – both are Core Web Vitals metrics Google uses.

Everything happens inside your browser tab. Your fonts are read from your disk into memory, processed there and saved straight back to your device. Nothing is uploaded, stored or logged, there is no account, and the tool keeps working offline once the page has loaded – so it is safe for private, confidential and unreleased material.
